title: PT1
lead: TryHackMe's Junior Penetration Tester cert. There's no multiple choice: you get 48 hours to attack a web app, a network and an Active Directory domain in a legal lab, capture flags, then write the professional report a client would read. It proves you can run a small pentest from start to finish.
objSub: Six topic areas from TryHackMe's PT1 training content. Tick objectives as you study them; progress saves on this device.
planSub: Set how many hours a week you can give it. The plan splits about 100 hours across the six areas, then saves the last stretch for full practice runs with a written report.
pbqSub: Hands-on practice in the style of the exam: read real tool output, then make the call a pentester would.
mockText: 25 items in 2.5 hours: 20 multiple-choice questions (200 points) and 5 hands-on Pentest Lab engagements (800 points), scored out of 1,000 with a pass mark of 750. It is different from the real exam: real PT1 is a 48-hour hands-on engagement across web, network and Active Directory with a graded report, and no multiple choice. Every attempt draws different questions and engagements, so retakes differ. Made-up targets only; practice real skills in legal labs.

cur.label: Current exam
cur.note: Three engagements, web application, network and Active Directory, each with its own scope and rules of engagement. You submit flags and write a report for each one. Candidates report a pass mark of 750 of 1000, with web worth the most.
cur.onote: TryHackMe lists these six areas without weights. The bars are a suggested study share, based on candidates reporting web at about 40% of the score, network about 36% and Active Directory about 24%.

domains.name: Reconnaissance and Enumeration
obj: WHOIS, DNS and subdomain discovery
Map the target's names and addresses before you touch anything else.
Nmap and port scanning strategies
Fast full-port sweeps first, then version and script scans on what's open.
Banner grabbing and service fingerprinting
Pin down exact software versions so you can look up known flaws.
Web and network account and service enumeration
Usernames, shares, directories, virtual hosts and API endpoints.
Exposed services and misconfigurations
Anonymous logins, default passwords, open shares and debug pages.

domains.name: Web Application Testing
obj: OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities
SQL injection, XSS, IDOR, SSRF and the rest, found and exploited by hand.
Manual testing techniques
Change one thing at a time and watch how the app responds.
Burp Suite
Proxy, Repeater, Intruder and Decoder: intercept, replay, fuzz and decode requests.
Authentication and session flaws
Weak logins, predictable tokens, missing logout and session fixation.
File upload and path traversal
Getting code onto the server, and reading files you shouldn't.
Bypassing client-side controls
Anything the browser enforces, the attacker can skip. Test the server.

domains.name: Network Penetration Testing
obj: SMB, RDP, FTP, SSH and SNMP
Find and exploit weak or misconfigured services on these ports.
Password attacks
Brute force and password spraying, and staying under the lockout limit.
Misconfigured and outdated services
Match versions to public exploits, and test default settings.
Pivoting and lateral movement
Use one compromised host to reach networks you couldn't before.
Sniffing, traffic analysis and man-in-the-middle
What you can capture on a network, and what it gives away.
Firewalls and network segmentation
Work out what's filtered, and find the paths that aren't.

domains.name: Active Directory Exploitation
obj: Kerberos attacks
AS-REP roasting and Kerberoasting, then cracking the hashes offline.
LDAP and domain enumeration
Users, groups, computers and policies, with or without credentials.
Misconfigured permissions and trusts
Rights like GenericAll or WriteDACL that hand you control of other objects.
Pass-the-hash and pass-the-ticket
Log in with a stolen hash or Kerberos ticket instead of a password.
Privilege escalation in a Windows domain
From a normal user to domain admin, one step at a time.
BloodHound
Graph the domain and find the shortest path to the account you want.

domains.name: Exploitation and Post-Exploitation
obj: Metasploit and manual exploitation
Use frameworks when they fit, and know how to do it by hand when they don't.
Reverse and bind shells
Which one gets through the firewall, and how to make a shell stable.
File transfer
Moving tools and loot with HTTP servers, SMB shares, certutil, wget and scp.
Persistence and staging
How attackers keep access, and why you document anything you add.
Privilege escalation on Linux and Windows
Sudo rights, SUID files, weak services and stored credentials.
Operational security
Stay inside the rules of engagement and leave the lab as you found it.

domains.name: Reporting and Time Management
obj: Clear vulnerability reports
What it is, where it is, how you proved it and what it lets an attacker do.
Prioritizing findings by risk
Rank by impact and how easy it is to exploit, not by how fun it was.
Relevant mitigations
A specific fix for the root cause, not 'apply best practices'.
Managing a 48-hour window
Plan sleep, set time limits per target and move on when you're stuck.
Note-taking during a test
Commands, output and screenshots as you go, so the report writes itself.
Communicating attack paths and impact
Tell the story from first foothold to the flag, in order.

extras.title: Your 48 hours
extras.sub: All areas · one engagement at a time
rows: Read the scope and rules of engagement for the section. Note what's off-limits.
Recon: full port scan, then versions and scripts on open ports.
Enumerate every service: web paths, shares, users, versions.
Exploit the most promising path. Time-box each idea to about an hour.
Escalate privileges and grab the flags. Screenshot every step.
Write that section's findings while it's fresh, then move on.
Last block: proofread the report. It's graded, not just the flags.

extras.title: Ports to check first
rows: Anonymous login, readable or writable files
Reused or weak passwords, keys you've found
The web app: most of the points
A domain controller. AS-REP roast and Kerberoast
Null sessions, open shares, signing off
Community strings like public leak users and processes
Logins with sprayed or found credentials

extras.title: AD attacks at a glance
rows: Accounts with Kerberos pre-authentication turned off hand out a crackable hash (hashcat mode 18200).
Request tickets for accounts with an SPN and crack them offline (hashcat mode 13100).
One or two common passwords across every user, staying under the lockout limit.
Log in with the hash itself. No cracking needed.
Collect the domain's relationships and find the shortest path to Domain Admins.

extras.title: Anatomy of a finding
rows: What an attacker can do with it
Exact requests and commands, in order
A specific fix for the root cause

method: Use the six areas above as your checklist. Web app testing is worth the most, so give it the most time.
Work through TryHackMe's Jr Penetration Tester path, plus the Active Directory rooms it points to.
Hack legal labs only: TryHackMe, Hack The Box and your own virtual machines. Write a mini report for every box.
Flashcards for ports, Nmap flags, Burp tools, hashcat modes and the AD attacks above.
Do a timed 48-hour practice run on a few unseen boxes, report included, before you book.
tips: Sleep is part of the plan
48 hours isn't a 48-hour sprint. Plan two real sleeps and you'll find more.
If an idea goes nowhere after an hour, write it down and try another path.
Screenshot each step and write the finding right away. Rebuilding notes at hour 46 is how people fail.
Reports are graded against a structure, so match TryHackMe's recommended layout for each finding.
Every section has its own rules of engagement. Read them before you scan anything.

quiz.q: A default Nmap scan of 10.10.5.20 shows only 22 and 80 open. The scope summary says the host also runs an admin service. What should you do next?
o: Scan all 65,535 TCP ports, for example nmap -p- --min-rate 1000, then run -sV -sC on anything new
Right. Without -p, Nmap only checks the 1,000 most common ports. Admin services often sit on high ports like 8443 or 10000.
Run a UDP scan of the top 100 ports
UDP is worth a look later, but an admin web service is almost always TCP. Check all TCP ports first.
Start brute-forcing SSH on 22
You haven't finished enumerating. Brute force is slow, noisy and usually the last resort.
Run nmap -sn to confirm the host is up
-sn is a ping sweep with no port scan, and you already know the host is up.

quiz.q: robots.txt on the target contains Disallow: /dev-backup/. What does that mean for your test?
o: It's a lead worth checking. robots.txt only asks search engines to stay away; it doesn't block anyone
Right. robots.txt is a polite request to crawlers, not access control. Disallowed paths often point at the interesting parts of a site.
The folder is protected and out of reach
Nothing in robots.txt protects a folder. Browse to it and see.
It's out of scope because the owner disallowed it
Scope comes from your rules of engagement, not from robots.txt.
It means the site has no other hidden folders
It lists only what the owner chose to list. Keep running content discovery.

quiz.q: Logged in as bob, GET /api/invoices/1043 shows your invoice. Changing it to 1042 returns another customer's invoice. What is it, and what's the fix?
o: IDOR (broken access control). The server must check that the invoice belongs to the logged-in user
Right. The app trusts the ID you send. The fix is a server-side ownership check on every request; random IDs alone only hide the problem.
SQL injection. Use parameterized queries
Nothing here changes a database query. You asked for a valid ID that just isn't yours.
Cross-site request forgery. Add CSRF tokens
CSRF tricks a victim's browser into sending a request. Here you read someone else's data directly.
Session fixation. Rotate session IDs at login
Your session is fine. The app never checks who owns the invoice.

quiz.q: An upload form only accepts images. You upload shell.php, change the Content-Type in Burp to image/png, and it's saved to /uploads/shell.php, where it runs. What's the root cause?
o: The server trusts the Content-Type header the client sends instead of checking the file itself and where it's stored
Right. Content-Type is set by the client, so you control it. The fix: check the real file type and extension on the server, rename files, and store uploads where they can't run.
The browser's file picker allowed .php files
Client-side checks don't matter. You can send any request with Burp.
The file was too large
Size has nothing to do with whether code runs.
The upload used HTTP instead of HTTPS
HTTPS protects the connection, not what the server does with the file.

quiz.q: A 'fetch URL preview' feature lets you submit any address. Submitting http://127.0.0.1:8080/admin returns the internal admin page. Which vulnerability is this?
o: Server-side request forgery (SSRF)
Right. You made the server send a request on your behalf to a place you can't reach yourself.
Cross-site scripting (XSS)
XSS runs your script in another user's browser. Here the server made the request.
Cross-site request forgery (CSRF)
CSRF makes a victim's browser send a request. Here it's the server doing it.
Directory traversal
Traversal reads files through a path. You're reaching an internal web service through a URL.

quiz.q: UDP port 161 is open on a printer, and the community string public works. Which tool gives you the most from it?
o: snmpwalk (or snmp-check) with community public, to dump users, processes and network info
Right. SNMP with a default community string will often hand over running processes, user names, routes and installed software.
smbclient -L
That lists SMB shares on 139/445, not SNMP.
hydra against SSH
There's no SSH here, and brute force isn't needed when SNMP is open.
Gobuster
Gobuster brute-forces web paths and DNS names. It doesn't speak SNMP.

quiz.q: The rules of engagement say accounts lock after 5 failed logins in 30 minutes. You have 300 usernames. Which password attack fits BEST?
o: Password spraying: try one or two likely passwords against every user, spaced out to stay under the limit
Right. Spraying tries few passwords across many users, so no single account hits the lockout limit.
Brute-force each user with rockyou.txt
That locks out every account after five guesses, which can break the client's business and violates the rules.
Brute-force only the administrator account
Five guesses won't get far, and locking the admin out is worse.
Credential stuffing with one leaked list per user
Still many guesses per account, so you'd hit the lockout.

quiz.q: You have a list of domain usernames but no password. Which attack can still give you something crackable?
o: AS-REP roasting accounts that don't require Kerberos pre-authentication
Right. For those accounts, the domain controller hands out data encrypted with the user's password without any login. Crack it offline with hashcat mode 18200.
Kerberoasting
Kerberoasting needs a working domain account to request service tickets.
Pass-the-hash
You don't have a hash yet.
DCSync
DCSync needs replication rights, which only highly privileged accounts have.

quiz.q: BloodHound shows your user is in HelpDesk, and HelpDesk has GenericAll over the IT-Admins group, whose members are local admins on the file server. What's the shortest path?
o: Use GenericAll to add yourself to IT-Admins, then log in to the file server as a local admin
Right. GenericAll is full control over the group, including changing its members. Add yourself, then use the group's rights.
Kerberoast the members of IT-Admins
That might work if they have SPNs and weak passwords, but you already have a direct path.
Run DCSync from your workstation
Nothing in that path gives you replication rights.
Reset the krbtgt password
You have no rights over krbtgt, and it's far outside what the path gives you.

quiz.q: The target can make outbound connections, but its firewall blocks all inbound ports except 80. You can run one command on it. Which shell is MOST likely to work?
o: A reverse shell: the target connects out to your listener
Right. Outbound traffic is allowed, so make the target call you. Port 443 or 80 on your end blends in.
A bind shell on port 4444
The target would listen on 4444, and the firewall blocks inbound traffic to it.
A bind shell on port 80
80 is already used by the web server, so you can't bind to it.
RDP to the target
RDP needs inbound 3389, which is blocked.

quiz.q: On a Linux foothold, sudo -l shows: (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/vim. What's the fastest way to root?
o: sudo vim -c ':!/bin/sh' to get a root shell from inside vim
Right. vim can run shell commands, and sudo runs vim as root, so the shell is root too. GTFOBins lists this.
Edit /etc/shadow with vim to crack root's hash
You could edit files as root, but cracking a hash is slow. The shell escape is instant.
Look for a kernel exploit
Kernel exploits can crash the box. Easy sudo rights come first.
sudo su
Your rule only allows vim, so sudo su will ask for a password and fail.

quiz.q: You found two issues: an unauthenticated SQL injection on the public login page that dumps all password hashes, and a missing security header on an internal page. How should they appear in the report?
o: SQL injection first, rated critical, with steps, evidence and a specific fix; the header as low
Right. Rank by impact and how easy it is to exploit. Anyone on the internet can use the injection to steal every password hash.
Both as high, so the client fixes everything
Inflating ratings makes the report less useful. Clients need to know what to fix first.
In the order you found them
Order by risk, not by when you found them.
Leave the header out, since it's minor
Report it, just rated low. Leaving findings out makes the report incomplete.

pbqs.title: Name the opening from the tool output
pbqs.scenario: Each snippet comes from an authorized lab engagement. Pick the opening it shows. Each answer is used once; two choices are distractors.

items.log:
161/udp open  snmp  SNMPv1 server; community: public
| snmp-info:
|   enterprise: net-snmp
|_  engineIDFormat: unknown
items.why: SNMP answers with the default community public. Walk it with snmpwalk to pull users, processes and network details.

items.log:
Anonymous login successful

  Sharename       Type      Comment
  ---------       ----      -------
  IT_Backup       Disk      Nightly configs
  IPC$            IPC       Remote IPC
items.why: -N means no password, and it still listed shares. Connect to IT_Backup and look for configs with credentials in them.

items.src: Burp Repeater · logged in as bob
items.log:
GET /api/orders/5512 HTTP/1.1
Cookie: session=bob...

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
{"order":5512,"owner":"alice","card_last4":"4417"}
items.why: Bob's session reads Alice's order just by changing the number. The server never checks who owns the order.

items.log:
[-] User jlee doesn't have UF_DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH set
$krb5asrep$23$svc_print@CORP.LOCAL:7f3a9c...e21b
items.why: svc_print doesn't require pre-authentication, so you got its AS-REP without a password. Crack it with hashcat mode 18200.

items.log:
User www-data may run the following commands on web01:
    (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/vim
items.why: vim can run shell commands, and sudo runs it as root. sudo vim -c ':!/bin/sh' gives a root shell.
The page parameter is included from the file system, and ../ walks out of the web folder. Read config files next for credentials.

pbqs.title: Rate each finding and pick the fix
pbqs.scenario: You're writing the report. For each finding, pick a severity and the fix that addresses the root cause. Each fix is used once.

rows.req: Unauthenticated SQL injection on the internet-facing login page. It dumps every user's password hash.
rows.why: Anyone on the internet can exploit it with no account, and it exposes every credential. That's critical. Parameterized queries fix the root cause.

rows.req: Logged-in customers can read other customers' orders, including names and addresses, by changing the order number.
rows.why: It needs a login, but any customer can read everyone's data. That's high. The fix is checking ownership on the server for every request.

rows.req: SMB signing isn't required on internal file servers, so captured logins can be relayed by someone already inside the network.
rows.why: Serious, but the attacker must already be inside the network, so it's usually medium. Require signing on every host.

rows.req: The public web server's banner shows Apache/2.4.58.
rows.why: It only helps an attacker pick exploits. Low. Turn off version details in the server banner.

mapSub: PT1 is hands-on proof you can run a small pentest. Pair it with PenTest+, which DoD billets recognize. Tap any cert to jump to it.

keep.text: TryHackMe certs are valid for 3 years from the day you start the exam. Today you renew by passing the exam again.
keep.after: TryHackMe says renewal through a more advanced cert or related rooms is coming.

keep.text: PT1 isn't on the DoD 8140 qualification matrix (V3.0). On its own it won't qualify you for a coded billet.
keep.after: PenTest+ is on the matrix, for roles like Vulnerability Assessment Analyst (541). PT1 is great practice before it.

keep.text: A practical exam with a graded report is strong proof for junior pentest interviews. Add the badge with its verify link.
keep.after: Bring a sanitized sample report from a practice lab to interviews. It shows you can explain what you found.

keep.text: Testing a system without written permission is a federal crime under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. Practice only in legal labs and on machines you own.
keep.after: On Coast Guard networks, only authorized assessment teams test. Never scan a work network to practice.
